extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in literary theory and Bakhtinian concepts
extracted.subtask_description: Use Bakhtin's theoretical concepts (dialogism, heteroglossia, polyphony, chronotope, carnivalesque, etc.) as criteria for analysing or producing literary works; the page explains what features make texts dialogic, polyphonic, carnivalesque, open, or chronotopic. Useful for writers and critics who want Bakhtinian evaluative standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogism
rubrics_metrics.description: All discourse is in essence a dialogical exchange; dialogism is a central claim of Bakhtin's philosophy of language and culture and it endows language with an ethical or ethico-political force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts by how they stage interaction between voices, perspectives, or discourses rather than presenting a single authoritative (monologic) perspective. Dialogic texts foreground relations, responses, and the ethical implications of addressivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteroglossia
rubrics_metrics.description: Heteroglossia is 'the base condition governing the operation of meaning in any utterance' — languages carry perspectival, evaluative, and ideological differences; an utterance appropriates the words of others and populates them with one's own intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work exhibits multiple social languages/points of view within utterances (not just vocabulary variation): presence of differing perspectives, ideologies, registers, and the contextual primacy over isolated textual signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyphony / Polyphonic novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Polyphony is 'a plurality of independent and unmerged voices and consciousnesses, a genuine polyphony of fully valid voices' — a novel form in which characters speak with autonomous voices rather than being subsumed under a single authorial consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge novels by the autonomy and validity of characters' voices, the coexistence (and interaction) of multiple consciousnesses, and whether the author resists finalizing or reducing those voices to an authoritative position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfinalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfinalizability: 'Nothing conclusive has yet taken place in the world... the world is open and free' — on the individual level, people can never be entirely externally defined; characters are always 'on the threshold' and never fully enclosed by objectifying definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer portrayals that leave characters and meanings open-ended, emphasize moments of crisis or turning points, and resist closure or totalizing explanations; critique works that finalize or objectify human subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnivalization / Carnivalesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnivalization describes techniques that subvert normal hierarchies, social roles, and assumed truths in favor of a 'carnival sense of the world' — joyful relativity where opposites meet and express themselves on equal footing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify features that invert authority or conventional order (role reversals, festive subversion, ambivalence, excess) and create threshold situations enabling creative interaction and dialogic exchange; consider carnivalization as a means to resist reification and finalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque realism is defined as a literary mode focused on the meaning of the body and the material 'lower bodily stratum' (the body’s processes), often linked to carnival and to a therapeutic, liberating laughter ('laughing truth' that degrades power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for imagery and scenes that emphasize bodily materiality, the lower body, bodily excess, and laughter as a form of social critique; evaluate whether such elements function to subvert authority or to recuperate suppressed popular modes of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menippean satire characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Menippean satire (as discussed by Bakhtin) includes intensified comicality, freedom from established constraints, bold use of fantastic situations to test truth, abrupt changes, inserted genres and multi-tonality, parodies, oxymorons, scandal scenes, inappropriate behaviour, and a sharp satirical focus on contemporary ideas and issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing a text as Menippean, check for these formal and tonal features: genre-mixing, abrupt shifts, satirical targeting of ideas, comic excess, and multi-voiced tonalities that refuse single-genre constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronotope (forms of time and of the chronotope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronotope literally means 'time-space' and is 'the intrinsic connectedness of temporal and spatial relationships that are artistically expressed in literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a narrative configures time and space together to produce meaning — the specific spatiotemporal structures (settings, temporal flow, narrative moments) that shape character action and thematic import; consider how chronotopic choices create the novel's world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel's distinctiveness (novel vs epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Bakhtin, the novel is distinct from the epic in that it flourishes on diversity and can 'embrace, ingest, and devour other genres' while other genres (epic) attempt to eliminate diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a work's genre-flexibility and capacity to incorporate multiple registers/genres; view the novel as a form suited to heteroglossia and diversity, and critique works that attempt epic-like totalization of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech genres — primary vs secondary genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres exist in communication; Bakhtin distinguishes primary genres (everyday, constitutive speech forms that legislate acceptable words/phrases in life) from secondary genres (more complex, composed types of text such as legal, scientific, literary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how different communicative genres operate within a text and how extraliterary (everyday) genres inform literary forms. Evaluate interplay between primary (utterance-level) and secondary (text-level) genres in shaping meaning and social orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tertiary nature of dialogue / three variables shaping utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers shape an utterance according to three variables: the object of discourse, the immediate addressee, and a 'superaddressee' — Bakhtin's tertiary model of dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying or composing utterances, consider whose voice is addressed, what is being discussed, and the implied larger audience or evaluative authority; good dialogic writing attends to these three shaping variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyglossia and intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Bakhtin emphasizes the hybrid nature of language (polyglossia) and the relation between utterances (intertextuality); meaning arises from context and the interplay of multiple language strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the text's intertextual networks, multilingual/heteroglossic strata, and how it incorporates or repurposes other voices and discourses; value works that foreground contextual relations over isolated signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial stance and methodological implications (dialogics vs dialectic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bakhtin distinguishes dialogics from dialectic, emphasizes the difference between the text and the aesthetic object, and critiques Formalists and Structuralists for oversimplifying content or rigidly adhering to 'code.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authorial methods: does the author privilege dialogic multiplicity and context over closed systemic codes? For methodology, prefer approaches that keep content, context, and ethical dialogic relations central rather than reducing texts to formal codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation plurality / avoidance of narrow interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bakhtin argues that interpretation has endless possibilities; narrow interpretations weaken the richness of the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage plural, context-aware readings; be skeptical of reductive single-axis interpretations. Value readings that preserve multiplicity and openness of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and recovery of suppressed language (Rabelaisian openness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Rabelais studies Bakhtin aims to recover sections of texts that were ignored or suppressed and to analyse the balance between language that was permitted and language that was not; openness is both analytic goal and textual quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing texts, look for recuperation of marginalized or suppressed voices/languages and an openness to registers normally excluded by official culture; value recuperative practices and exposure of censorious limits.
